question_interpretation: Asks what 21 CFR Part 820 (QMSR) covers and which manufacturers are subject to it.

issues.detail: The question asks 'which manufacturers are subject to it'. J lists only the covered activities; it omits that any manufacturer engaged in those activities for a finished device must comply, that subject manufacturers expressly include contract sterilizers, installers, relabelers, remanufacturers, repackers, specification developers and initial distributors of foreign entities (820.1(a)), and that a manufacturer doing only some operations complies only with the requirements for those operations.

820.1(a)(1) (applies to finished devices for human use manufactured in the U.S./territories or imported or offered for import) and the express carve-outs in 820.1(a)(2) (component/part manufacturers) and (a)(3) (blood and blood components) define who is subject but are not in G or J. The 820.3(b) definition of 'manufacturer' is also relevant.

Clause 4.1 as the QMS 'general requirements' clause is corroborated by 21 CFR 4.4(b)(1)(i). Clause 1's role (application/permissible exclusions) is described in the QMSR preamble, but the title 'Scope' is not stated in FDA text; that part of H/I rests on general knowledge.

explanation: 820.1(a) supports J's list of activities and the 'QMS appropriate for its specific device(s)' element. But J does not answer the second half of the question (which manufacturers), which 820.1(a) answers explicitly. It also omits the (a)(1) geographic and import reach and the (a)(2)/(a)(3) exclusions. The citation is right but incomplete.
proposed_corrected_answer: Part 820 sets CGMP (QMSR) requirements for the methods, facilities and controls used in the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use. Any manufacturer engaged in any of those activities for a finished device must establish and maintain a QMS appropriate for its specific device(s). This expressly includes contract sterilizers, installers, relabelers, remanufacturers, repackers, specification developers and initial distributors of foreign entities. A manufacturer engaged in only some operations complies only with the requirements for those operations. It applies to finished devices for human use made in the U.S. (States, Territories, DC, Puerto Rico) or imported or offered for import (820.1(a)(1)). It does not apply to component/part manufacturers (820.1(a)(2)) or to blood and blood component manufacturers (820.1(a)(3)).

question_interpretation: Asks what Part 820 provides for foreign manufacturers that refuse to permit an FDA inspection.

issues.detail: The key reflects the pre-QMSR text: former 820.1(d) provided that a foreign manufacturer's refusal to permit or complete an FDA inspection made it appear, for section 801(a), that its devices were nonconforming and adulterated. The QMSR (effective 2026-02-02) replaced it. Current 820.1(c) says only that an imported device is subject to refusal of admission under 801(a) if, among other things, it appears to be adulterated. Current Part 820 no longer addresses refusal of inspection.

The link between refusing inspection and refusal of admission now runs through statute. FD&C Act 501(j) (21 U.S.C. 351(j)) deems a drug or device adulterated if the establishment delays, denies or limits an inspection or refuses entry or inspection. Section 801(a) (21 U.S.C. 381(a)) then allows refusal of admission of adulterated articles. G omits 501(j).

The question presumes Part 820 has an inspection-refusal provision for foreign manufacturers. A correct current answer should say that 820.1(c) is framed in terms of apparent adulteration under 801(a), not refusal of inspection. FDA's preamble states the revision aligns with sections 501 and 801 and does not change foreign manufacturers' obligations.

explanation: J's bottom line (refusal to permit inspection can lead to refusal of admission) remains legally true, because 501(j) makes such devices adulterated and 801(a)/820.1(c) allow refusal of admission of devices that appear adulterated. But J attributes that rule to Part 820 itself, and that is the former 820.1(d) text, which the QMSR removed. The current paragraph (820.1(c)) does not mention inspection refusal. The key needs the current wording and the 501(j) link.
proposed_corrected_answer: Current Part 820 (QMSR) no longer has a specific inspection-refusal provision. 820.1(c) provides that an imported or offered-for-import device is subject to refusal of admission under FD&C Act 801(a) if, among other things, it appears to be adulterated. A device from an establishment whose owner, operator or agent delays, denies or limits an inspection, or refuses to permit entry or inspection, is adulterated under FD&C Act 501(j). It can therefore be refused admission under 801(a). (Before 2026-02-02, former 820.1(d) expressly tied refusal of a foreign-facility inspection to 801(a) nonconformity and 501(h) adulteration.)

question_interpretation: Asks which definitions apply to Part 820 and which prevail in a conflict.

issues.detail: J omits that 820.3(a) adds FDA definitions for terms not used or not defined in ISO 13485/ISO 9000 (batch or lot, component, FD&C Act, finished device, HCT/P regulated as a device, remanufacturer). G cites 820.3(a) but J does not use it.

Precedence has two layers. FD&C Act 201 definitions supersede correlating ISO 13485 terms (e.g., device, labeling). The further 820.3(b) terms (implantable medical device, manufacturer, organization, rework, safety and performance) supersede correlating terms in ISO 13485 or ISO 9000. J mentions only the 201 layer and says 'standard terms' generally. The introductory text also says the incorporated definitions 'do not affect the meaning of similar terms defined in this title'.

explanation: The introductory text of 820.3 and 820.3(b) support J's three elements. J omits the 820.3(a) supplementary definitions, which G itself cites, and the 820.3(b) list of FDA-specified terms that supersede ISO definitions, so it only partly answers 'which definitions apply'. H is corroborated: FDA's preamble identifies Clause 3 of ISO 13485 as its terms-and-definitions clause, and 820.7(a) names ISO 9000 'Clause 3—Terms and definitions'.
proposed_corrected_answer: The definitions in ISO 13485 and in Clause 3 of ISO 9000:2015 (IBR, 820.7) apply, except as specified in 820.3(b), and do not affect the meaning of similar terms defined elsewhere in Title 21. 820.3(a) adds definitions for terms not used or defined in those standards (batch or lot, component, FD&C Act, finished device, HCT/P regulated as a device, remanufacturer). Under 820.3(b), all FD&C Act section 201 definitions apply and supersede correlating ISO 13485 terms (e.g., device and labeling in 201(h) and (m)). FDA's definitions of implantable medical device, manufacturer, organization, rework and safety and performance supersede correlating ISO 13485/ISO 9000 terms.

question_interpretation: Asks what meaning Part 820 gives the ISO 13485 term 'safety and performance'.

issues.detail: 820.3(b) gives 'safety and performance' the meaning of 'safety and effectiveness' only in Clause 0.1 of ISO 13485. FDA deliberately narrowed this from the proposed rule ('to apply only to Clause 0.1'). J states the equivalence for the term generally 'as used in the incorporated standard', without the Clause 0.1 limitation.

J omits the second sentence of the definition: the phrase does not relieve a manufacturer of any obligation to implement controls that provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness. 820.1(a) adds that other terminology such as 'safety and performance' does not change the statutory safety-and-effectiveness standard.
The preamble ties the meaning to section 520(f) of the FD&C Act, not to the FD&C Act and FDA regulations generally.

explanation: 820.3(b) is the right citation. But the definition is expressly limited to Clause 0.1 of ISO 13485, and FDA's preamble stresses that the two phrases are not interchangeable and that the clarification applies only within Clause 0.1. J's unqualified equivalence overstates the rule and omits the 'does not relieve' sentence. H (0.1 General; 3) is corroborated by 820.3(b) and the preamble.
proposed_corrected_answer: Under 820.3(b), 'safety and performance' has the meaning of 'safety and effectiveness' in Clause 0.1 of ISO 13485 only; FDA explains it means assessing device performance to assure the device is safe and effective as required by FD&C Act 520(f). The phrase does not relieve a manufacturer of any obligation to implement controls or other measures that provide reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness. 820.1(a) confirms that such terminology does not change the statutory safety-and-effectiveness standard.

question_interpretation: Asks what 21 CFR 820.10 as a whole requires of a manufacturer subject to Part 820.

issues.detail: The question asks what 820.10 requires. Besides (a), 820.10 requires compliance with other applicable Title 21 requirements to fully comply with listed ISO clauses: UDI per part 830, tracking per part 821 if applicable, MDR per part 803, advisory notices per part 806 ((b)(1)-(4)). It also requires design and development (Clause 7.3) for class II, class III and listed class I devices ((c)) and Clause 7.5.9.2 traceability for life-supporting/sustaining devices ((d)), and makes non-compliance adulteration under 501(h) ((e)). J and G cover only (a).

FDA's preamble states 'all sections of ISO 13485 apply'. 4.4(b)(1)(i) links Clause 4.1 to general requirements and Clause 5 to management responsibility. FDA text does not state the titles 'Resource management', 'Product realization' and 'Measurement, analysis and improvement' for clauses 6-8; those rest on general knowledge. Limiting H to 4-8 also leaves out Clause 1 (permissible exclusions), which FDA links to 820.10(c).

explanation: 820.10(a) supports J's single element. But 820.10 has four more operative paragraphs ((b)-(e)) with distinct obligations, and the question asks about the section as a whole. An answer citing only (a) would miss most of the section, and a complete answer citing (b)-(e) would be under-rewarded on citation scoring. H's clause titles are only partly corroborated by FDA text.
proposed_corrected_answer: A manufacturer subject to Part 820 (as described in 820.1(a)) must: (a) document a QMS that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (IBR, 820.7) and other applicable requirements of Part 820. (b) Comply, as appropriate, with other applicable Title 21 requirements to fully comply with the listed ISO clauses: UDI system per part 830 (Clause 7.5.8), traceability procedures per part 821 if applicable (7.5.9.1), notify FDA of complaints meeting part 803 criteria (8.2.3), and handle advisory notices per part 806 (7.2.3, 8.2.3, 8.3.3). (c) Comply with design and development (Clause 7.3) for class II, class III and the listed class I devices. (d) For devices that support or sustain life, comply with Clause 7.5.9.2 traceability. (e) Failure to comply renders the device adulterated under FD&C Act 501(h), and the device and responsible persons are subject to regulatory action.

question_interpretation: Asks what 21 CFR 820.35 adds to ISO 13485 Clause 4.2.5 record-control requirements.

issues.detail: J says only that 820.35 is an FDA supplement specifying additional record content. The question asks what it adds. The substance is: (a) complaint records (review, evaluation and investigation; justification when a similar complaint was already investigated; seven data items for MDR-reportable/investigated complaints), (b) servicing records (six minimum items), (c) the UDI recorded for each device or batch, and (d) confidentiality marking of records for part 20 disclosure decisions.
G cites only the introductory text; the operative additions are in 820.35(a)-(d).

explanation: The 820.35 introductory text supports the framing in J (and H 4.2.5 Control of records is corroborated by it). J's element is generic, though, and would accept an answer that names none of the actual additional requirements. Those requirements are in paragraphs (a)-(d), which G does not cite.
proposed_corrected_answer: In addition to ISO 13485 Clause 4.2.5 (Control of Records), 820.35 requires certain record content. (a) Complaint records: records of review, evaluation and investigation of complaints involving possible failure of a device, labeling or packaging to meet specifications, and a documented justification when no investigation is performed because a similar complaint was already investigated. For MDR-reportable, must-investigate and investigated complaints, record the device name, date received, UDI/UPC/other identification, complainant name/address/phone, nature and details, any correction or corrective action, and any reply. (b) Servicing records: device name, UDI/UPC/other identification, service date, who serviced it, service performed, and test and inspection data. (c) The UDI recorded for each device or batch. (d) Records the manufacturer deems confidential may be marked to aid FDA's part 20 disclosure determinations.

820.35(a) ties the justification record to one situation: no new investigation because an investigation was already performed for a similar complaint. J's 'justification when no investigation is made' is broader than the regulatory text.

explanation: 820.35(a) supports J's first element (records of review, evaluation and investigation) and, in narrower form, the justification element. proposed_corrected_answer: Under 820.35(a), the manufacturer must keep records of the review, evaluation and investigation of any complaint involving the possible failure of a device, labeling or packaging to meet its specifications. If a similar complaint was already investigated, another investigation is not necessary, but the manufacturer must keep records justifying not investigating. For complaints reportable under part 803, complaints it determines must be investigated, and complaints it investigated anyway, it must record: (1) device name; (2) date received; (3) any UDI or UPC and other device identification; (4) complainant name, address and phone; (5) nature and details of the complaint; (6) any correction or corrective action; (7) any reply to the complainant.
